sections.title: 13. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Q&A

**Q1. What is the difference between a log, a metric, and a trace?**
A log is a discrete event record (one thing happened). A metric is an aggregated numeric measurement over time (count, sum, histogram). A trace is a causal tree of spans showing how one request flowed through the system. Logs answer "what happened?", metrics answer "how much and how fast?", traces answer "why did this request behave this way?"

**Q2. What is a span, and what is the minimum set of attributes it should carry?**
A span is one unit of work in a trace. Minimum: name, start_time, end_time, status, trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id. For AI spans, add model, input, output, token counts, and cost.

**Q3. Why is OpenTelemetry a good foundation for AI tracing?**
OTel is vendor-neutral with language SDKs and a wire format (OTLP) supported by every major backend. Instrument once in OTel and you can switch from Jaeger to Langfuse to Datadog without re-instrumenting. For AI specifically, OpenLLMetry and OpenInference layer AI semantic conventions on top.

**Q4. How do LangSmith and Langfuse differ?**
LangSmith is LangChain-native with the tightest LangChain/LangGraph integration and built-in eval + datasets. Langfuse is open-source, vendor-neutral, OTel-compatible, and self-hostable. Choose LangSmith if you're all-in on LangChain; choose Langfuse for framework-agnostic or self-hosted setups.

**Q5. What are the three main sampling strategies, and when do you use each?**
Head-based (decide upfront — cheap, misses rare errors), tail-based (decide after — best for catching failures, requires buffering), and stratified (always keep errors + small % of success + 100% of specific experiments — what most production teams converge on).

**Q6. Why isn't logging enough for AI systems?**
One user request fans out into many LLM calls, tool calls, and retrievals. Logs record each in isolation; you lose the causal chain that tells you which call caused which output. Traces preserve parent/child structure across the whole request, which is what you need to debug "why did the bot say that?"

**Q7. What is context propagation, and why does it matter for AI?**
Context propagation carries the trace ID and current parent span ID across process, thread, async, and service boundaries (typically via the W3C `traceparent` header). Without it, a request crossing a service boundary becomes two disconnected traces and the causal chain breaks — critical for AI where orchestration often spans multiple services.

**Q8. What is trace-based eval, and how does it differ from static-dataset eval?**
Trace-based eval samples real production traces and scores them (per-span and per-trace) instead of running against a frozen golden set. It tracks distribution drift and grounds eval in production. Static datasets are reproducible but age out; trace-based eval stays current but needs sampling and PII redaction.

**Q9. How would you redact PII from traces before export?**
Combine strategies: regex for known patterns (emails, phones, SSNs), NER for entity-level PII, and field allowlists for high-risk spans. Redact at the collector before export, never after. For the highest-risk spans, drop `input`/`output` entirely and keep only metadata.

**Q10. What is the difference between OpenLLMetry and OpenInference?**
OpenLLMetry (Traceloop) produces OTel instrumentation for AI libraries — it's the SDK layer. OpenInference (Arize) defines semantic conventions for AI span attributes — it's the spec layer. They're complementary: OpenLLMetry emits spans; OpenInference says what attributes those spans should carry for AI eval.

### B. Scenario-Based Questions

**Scenario 1.** Your production support agent hallucinates a refund policy number in roughly 1% of conversations. Users complain; customer success escalates. You have CloudWatch logs but no tracing. How do you find the root cause?

**Task**: Describe the investigation plan.

**Sample Answer**: First, add tracing — even minimal spans around each LLM and tool call — and ship it to production. Within a day, sample traces from conversations users flagged as wrong. Walk through 5–10 failing traces top-to-bottom: read each retrieve span's docs, each tool call's args and results, each generate span's input and output. Look for the pattern: off-topic retrieved docs? Stale tool data? Missing system-prompt context? Once you find a common shape (say, retrieve spans returning docs with relevance < 0.2), narrow to that shape across all traces and confirm the same root cause in 80%+ of cases. Then implement a fix (relevance threshold, better retrieval, or a final-answer faithfulness guard) and re-trace to confirm the hallucination rate dropped.

**Scenario 2.** Your tracing bill is $5,000/month, mostly object storage for full trace payloads. Leadership wants it cut to $1,500 without losing debugging ability. What do you do?

**Task**: Propose a specific plan.

**Sample Answer**: Move to stratified tail-based sampling: keep 100% of error traces, 100% above p99 latency, 100% tagged with active experiment IDs, and 1% of everything else. This typically cuts volume 80–90% while preserving every trace you'd actually debug. Second, redact `input`/`output` on the 1% sample (keep them on errors and experiments) to shrink payload size. Third, set a TTL of 30 days for sampled success traces and 90 days for error traces. Fourth, drop low-value attributes (verbose retrieved-doc full text) and keep only `doc_ids` plus a relevance score. Combined, these moves usually land you under $1,500 while preserving debugging fidelity.

**Scenario 3.** Tracing shows p50 latency = 1.0s but p95 = 8.0s for the same endpoint. The product feels fine for most users but terrible for the unlucky 5%. Investigate.

**Task**: Lay out the diagnostic.

**Sample Answer**: The p50/p95 gap means a long-tail subset of traces is structurally different, not just slower. Slice by span name: which span has the largest p95/p50 ratio? Likely candidates are retries, tool calls to external APIs, or a second retrieval pass. Then group the slow traces by trace shape — are they deeper (more agent steps)? Do they have `retry=true`? Do they cluster on a specific `experiment_id` or `user_id`? Common causes: a flaky external tool that times out and retries (fix with circuit breaker + faster timeout), an agent looping on a specific query pattern (fix with max-iterations guard + better stopping criterion), or a retrieval path re-running on low-confidence hits (fix by caching or tightening the confidence threshold). The trace is your evidence; you're looking for the structural difference between the slow 5% and the fast 95%.

**Scenario 4.** Your VP of Engineering asks: "We already have Datadog APM with logs and metrics. Why do we need a separate AI tracing tool like Langfuse or Phoenix?"

**Task**: Respond in 5–8 sentences.

**Sample Answer**: APM tools are excellent for service-to-service latency and infra health but were not built for AI semantics. They don't natively model prompt-as-input, completion-as-output, token counts, cost-per-call, retrieved-doc relevance, or agent trajectories — you'd be cramming AI concepts into generic attributes and building the AI-specific views yourself. AI tracing tools (Langfuse, Phoenix, LangSmith) ship with first-class support for LLM-as-judge eval, datasets-from-traces, prompt management, and trajectory visualization, and they implement OpenInference semantic conventions so spans are queryable by `model`, `tokens_in`, `cost_usd`, etc. out of the box. The right architecture is usually both: OTel instrumentation feeding generic spans to Datadog for infra and AI-tagged spans (via OpenLLMetry) to Langfuse/Phoenix for AI eval. You're not replacing APM; you're adding an AI-aware layer that APM doesn't cover.

**Scenario 5.** You ship a new prompt version (v2) and the next morning your trace-based eval score drops from 0.86 to 0.71. But the prompt is barely different — just a wording tweak. How do you investigate?

**Task**: Diagnose using traces.

**Sample Answer**: Filter traces by `prompt_version=v2` and compare span-by-span against v1 traces on the same inputs. Look first at the cheapest explanation: did the wording change cause the retriever to surface different docs (reranker sensitivity to query phrasing)? Compare `retrieved_doc_ids` per query between v1 and v2. If docs are the same, look at the generate span: did the new wording shift the model toward shorter answers (lower recall) or hedging (lower faithfulness)? Compute per-span metrics: per-retrieval context precision, per-LLM-call faithfulness, per-tool-call success. The drop will localize to one span type. Often a "minor" wording tweak — say, removing an explicit "use only the provided context" instruction — causes the model to drift into parametric knowledge and tank faithfulness. The trace tells you which span moved; the prompt diff tells you why.
